title: Count Primes
description: Brute force to optimized: trial division per number versus the Sieve of Eratosthenes, then its two classic refinements.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a number n, count how many prime numbers exist that are strictly less than n.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Batch elimination, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, instead of individually testing each candidate for primality."],["Difficulty","Intermediate"],["Tags","Math"],["Interview Focus","Knowing the Sieve of Eratosthenes by name, and its two classic refinements: stop the outer loop at the square root of n, and start crossing out at p squared instead of 2p."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a number n, count how many prime numbers exist that are strictly less than n.

blocks.title: Analogy: Crossing Out Names on a Wall
blocks.text: Picture writing every number from 2 up to n minus 1 on a wall. Starting from 2, cross out every multiple of 2 except 2 itself. Move to the next number still standing, 3, and cross out every multiple of 3. Keep going with the next surviving number each time. Whatever numbers are never crossed out by the end are exactly the prime numbers, since a prime has no smaller factor to be crossed out by.

blocks.caption: Cross out multiples of each prime, count what survives

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 10
The primes less than 10 are 2, 3, 5, and 7, giving a count of 4.
Example: n = 0 and n = 1
There are no numbers at all to check below 0 or below 1, so both cases return 0.
Example: n = 2
Only the number 1 is less than 2, and 1 does not count as prime by definition, so the answer is 0.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what testing each candidate separately is throwing away.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Testing each candidate for primality independently, by trial division, completely ignores information already discovered about smaller numbers.

Observation 2: Once a number p is confirmed prime, every multiple of p, 2p, 3p, 4p, and so on, is automatically composite and never needs to be tested individually again.

Observation 3: Crossing out all of p's multiples in one sweep, rather than testing each multiple separately later, eliminates enormous amounts of duplicated work across all candidates at once.

Observation 4: This idea can be tightened further: the outer loop only needs to check candidates up to the square root of n, and crossing out a prime's multiples can safely start at its own square instead of twice itself.
That reasoning alone already points straight at the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and its two standard refinements.
6. Brute Force Solution
The most direct approach is to test every single candidate from 2 up to n minus 1, checking whether it has any divisor other than 1 and itself, by trial division up to its square root.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every candidate from 2 up to n minus 1.
Check whether it is divisible by any number from 2 up to its own square root.
If no divisor is found, count it as prime.
Return the total count.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: test every candidate independently by trial division

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: isPrime is written as its own dedicated helper specifically because it is called once per candidate, and testing divisibility only up to a candidate's own square root is a meaningful optimization worth isolating in its own function.

The trial division loop only checks divisors up to the square root of the candidate, since any factor larger than the square root must be paired with a factor smaller than it, meaning a divisor would already have been found by that point if one exists.

Every candidate from 2 up to n minus 1 is tested completely independently, with no information shared between candidates, which is deliberately what makes this version so much slower than the sieve based approaches that follow.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because trial division up to the square root is a correct, complete way to test primality for any single number.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times the square root of n), since every one of the n candidates is tested independently with its own trial division.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: testing every number independently repeats an enormous amount of work. When 2 is found to be prime, every multiple of 2 could immediately be marked as not prime without ever testing them individually, instead of re-discovering that fact one number at a time.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why testing each candidate independently works but is wasteful: confirming 2 is prime and confirming 4 is not prime are treated as two completely separate problems, even though 4 being a multiple of 2 already proves it composite.

What information is being thrown away: once a number is known prime, every one of its multiples is automatically known composite, with no further testing needed.

Can that knowledge be applied in bulk instead of per candidate: yes, sweeping through and marking every multiple of a confirmed prime handles all of them at once, instead of rediscovering compositeness one candidate at a time.

What is this technique called: the Sieve of Eratosthenes, one of the oldest known algorithms for this exact task.

The core idea: maintain a single boolean array, and whenever an unmarked number is found, mark all of its multiples as composite in one pass.

Instead of testing each candidate in isolation, mark composite numbers directly: once a number is known to be prime, cross out every one of its multiples in a single sweep, since none of them can possibly be prime.
This is the Sieve of Eratosthenes, one of the oldest and most efficient known ways to find all primes up to a limit.
9. Optimized Solution
Keep a boolean array tracking whether each number has been crossed out. For every number that is still unmarked, count it as prime and cross out all of its multiples, starting from twice itself.
Dry run for n = 10

blocks.text: Numbers 2, 3, 5, and 7 remain unmarked, giving a count of 4.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: cross out multiples in bulk instead of testing each number alone

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because every composite number has at least one prime factor smaller than or equal to it, and that prime factor will eventually be reached by the outer loop, since the outer loop walks upward from 2. The moment that prime factor is processed, every one of its multiples, including this composite number, gets marked, guaranteeing every composite number is crossed out by the time the loop finishes, leaving only true primes unmarked.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A number is never crossed out by any smaller prime's sweep","It has no factor smaller than itself other than 1","It is prime, gets counted, and its own multiples get crossed out next"],["A number is crossed out by some smaller prime's sweep","It is a multiple of that smaller prime","It is composite, correctly excluded from the final count"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The multiples-crossing loop starts at 2 times pnum, not pnum itself, since pnum is the prime being confirmed and must never be marked composite by its own sweep.
is_composite is sized to exactly n entries and initialized to all false, so every number starts assumed prime until some sweep proves otherwise.

Counting happens the moment an unmarked number is encountered in the outer loop, rather than in a separate final pass, since by the time the outer loop reaches a given number, every smaller prime's sweep has already had a chance to cross it out if it were composite.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: roughly O(n log n), since crossing out multiples of every prime up to n sums to a harmonic-like total.
Space: O(n), for the array tracking which numbers have been crossed out.
10. Further Optimization: Start at p Squared, Stop at the Square Root

Two refinements tighten the sieve further. First, the outer loop only ever needs to check p up to the square root of n, since any composite number less than n must have at least one factor that small. Second, when crossing out multiples of p, starting at 2p is wasteful, every multiple smaller than p squared (like 2p, 3p, up to (p minus 1)p) has already been crossed out by a smaller prime factor.
Dry run for n = 10

blocks.text: The outer loop stops after p = 3, having only needed to check up to the square root of 10, and still correctly identifies 4 primes.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: only sieve up to the square root, and start each prime at its own square

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The outer loop condition compares pnum times pnum against n, rather than pnum against n directly, since any composite number below n is guaranteed to have a prime factor at or below the square root of n, making every prime past that point unnecessary as a sweep starting point.

The inner sweep starts at pnum times pnum instead of 2 times pnum, since every smaller multiple of pnum is guaranteed to already have been crossed out by an even smaller prime factor before pnum was ever reached.

The final count is computed in a separate pass after the sieve loop finishes, since the outer loop itself now stops early at the square root of n and can no longer double as the counting pass the basic sieve used.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log log n), the standard tight bound for the Sieve of Eratosthenes, a real reduction in total work compared to the basic sieve.
Space: O(n), unchanged, the array is still needed to track every number up to n.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is shifting from testing each item individually to eliminating many items at once based on a shared property, exactly what the Sieve of Eratosthenes does with multiples of each prime. Stopping the outer loop at the square root of n, and starting each prime's elimination at its own square, are two classic refinements worth remembering for any sieve based solution.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that 1 is not a prime number, so the sieve and any counting should start from 2.
Starting the multiples crossing out loop at p instead of 2p, or p squared in the refined version, which would incorrectly mark p itself as composite.
Off by one errors with "strictly less than n" versus "less than or equal to n", since this problem specifically asks for primes below n, not including n.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is one of the clearest demonstrations of why "batch elimination" beats "individual testing" for problems involving many related checks. Knowing the Sieve of Eratosthenes by name, and being able to explain both of its standard refinements, is exactly the kind of classical algorithm knowledge interviewers like to see recognized quickly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid testing every number individually", think: the Sieve of Eratosthenes, crossing out multiples in bulk.
If the interviewer says "can the sieve be made tighter", think: stop the outer loop at the square root of n, and start each prime's sweep at its own square.
If the interviewer says "why can multiples below p squared be skipped", think: every one of them already has a smaller prime factor that would have crossed it out first.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is it safe to stop the outer sieve loop at the square root of n?
Why can crossing out a prime's multiples safely start at its own square instead of twice itself?
How would you find all primes in a specific range, say between two large numbers, instead of starting from 2 every time?
Can you reduce the sieve's space usage below O(n), for example by only tracking odd numbers?
What is the segmented sieve technique, and why is it useful when n is extremely large?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The segmented sieve, which applies this exact same batch-elimination idea to a specific range of numbers instead of always starting from 2.
Any "mark many related items at once instead of testing each individually" problem, the same batch elimination idea applied outside of primality.
Prime factorization problems in general, which often reuse a precomputed sieve, or a smallest-prime-factor array built the same way, to factorize many numbers quickly afterward.
Union-Find and other batch-processing structures, which share the broader theme of resolving many related facts together instead of one at a time.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force trial division approach runs in O(n times the square root of n) time and O(1) space. The basic sieve improves time to roughly O(n log n) at the cost of O(n) space. The refined sieve, stopping at the square root of n and starting each prime at its own square, tightens this further to the well known O(n log log n) bound, still using O(n) space.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: batch elimination, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, instead of individually testing each candidate for primality.

Core Idea: once a number is confirmed prime, every one of its multiples can be crossed out in a single sweep, and this sweep only ever needs to start from primes up to the square root of n, beginning each sweep at the prime's own square.
Time: O(n times the square root of n) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the basic sieve, O(n log log n) for the refined sieve.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for both sieve versions.
Most Important Observation: testing primality one candidate at a time throws away information that a single well organized sweep can reuse across every candidate at once.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write a correct but slow trial-division loop; knowing the Sieve of Eratosthenes by name, and its two standard refinements, is what is actually being tested.
One line memory trick: cross out multiples in bulk, start each prime's sweep at its own square, stop checking primes past the square root of n.
